extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of constitutional law, comparative politics, and readers of political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles governing judicial review, political jurisdiction (impeachment), and federal-state allocation of powers as presented in a comparative treatment of France, England, and the United States. Focuses on how institutions and procedures shape limits on government and the practical effects of those limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial right to refuse application of unconstitutional laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have acknowledged the right of the judges to found their decisions on the constitution rather than on the laws; in other words, they have left them at liberty not to apply such laws as may appear to them to be unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power is peculiar to the American magistrate and is explained by the nature of the American constitution (a supreme instrument that may be altered only by the people in predetermined cases). It confers immense political influence because when a judge refuses to apply a law in a case that law loses part of its moral cogency, encouraging further suits and potentially rendering the law powerless unless the people amend the constitution or the legislature repeals the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of judicial review to case-by-case adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges contest laws when those laws are argued in a tribunal of the United States and may refuse to admit them as a rule in a particular case; the judge decides the law only because obliged to judge a case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By tying censorship of the laws to private interests and particular lawsuits, judicial resistance is concealed from public gaze and avoids open political assaults on legislators. This procedural restraint reduces the political dangers of judicial power and protects legislation from wanton or partisan attacks that might follow from open judicial criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effects of judicial non-application on legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: From the time a judge has refused to apply any given law in a case, that law loses a portion of its moral cogency; similarly situated parties learn means exist to evade the law and suits multiply until it becomes powerless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two remedies follow: the people may alter the constitution or the legislature may repeal the law. The system reduces the risk of judges acting as open political actors, but enables incremental erosion of laws via repeated judicial non-application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen right to indict public functionaries before ordinary tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: In a free country like America all the citizens have the right of indicting public functionaries before the ordinary tribunals, and all the judges have the power of punishing public offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a natural right and seen as increasing respect for authorities and making public officers more scrupulous. Because lawsuits are difficult and expensive, only solid grounds will induce prosecution, which reduces frivolous political trials compared with mere press attacks; minor prosecutions available to the public are viewed as better safeguards of freedom than rare great judicial actions (impeachments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political jurisdiction defined as temporary legal authority of a political body
rubrics_metrics.description: Political jurisdiction is the temporary right of pronouncing a legal decision with which a political body may be invested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whereas in absolute governments extraordinary procedures add little, in free countries temporary confusion between functions (legislative bodies acting as judges) has been used to secure extraordinary adjudicative resources; different nations adapt this principle differently (England, France, United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment procedure: House impeaches, Senate tries; scope limited to public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the House of Representatives arraigns the offender, and the Senate awards his sentence; the Senate can only try such persons as are brought before it by the House and those persons must belong to the class of public functionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jurisdiction of the Senate is less extensive than that of European peers: political jurisdiction in the U.S. is chiefly administrative (removal from office and disqualification) rather than criminal punishment; if criminal punishment is sought (e.g., deprivation of liberty or life), ordinary courts and juries must be used after the political proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between European political tribunals and American political jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: In Europe political tribunals (House of Lords, Chambre des Pairs) may make use of all existing penal laws to punish delinquents; in the United States, when political bodies deprive an offender of official rank, their jurisdiction terminates and ordinary tribunals begin for criminal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European political jurisdiction acts as a full judicial sanction and may impose severe penalties, while American political jurisdiction is primarily an administrative measure to remove and disqualify officials, preserving milder but more readily applied sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of American political jurisdiction as preventive administrative measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The main object of the political jurisdiction in the United States is to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again; this is an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a political trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because removal and disqualification are less severe than criminal punishments, American political jurisdiction is applied more readily and regularly, making it an ordinary instrument of government rather than an extraordinary remedy for great offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk arising from broad descriptions of political offences and mild penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Article II, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution removes civil officers 'on impeachment for, and conviction of, treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors.' Many state constitutions use vaguer terms like 'misconduct or maladministration,' subjecting officers to unlimited responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mildness of American political penalties (removal rather than death or imprisonment) paradoxically makes them more formidable politically: removal is easy to pronounce, may be used for partisan ends, and is deeply harmful to honor and position; thus political jurisdiction can be a powerful tool of majorities and is readily abused when definitions of offenses are broad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of authority between Federal Government and States (enumerated powers principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attributes of the Federal Government were carefully enumerated and all that was not included amongst them was declared to constitute a part of the privileges of the several Governments of the States. The government of the States remained the rule, and that of the Confederation became the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Union was formed to meet general exigencies, its powers are few and defined (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce, etc.), while powers reserved to the States are numerous and indeterminate; when Congress neglects an enumerated power, states may legislate on that matter until Congress acts (example: bankruptcy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a high Federal court to maintain balance between Union and States
rubrics_metrics.description: A high Federal court was created which was destined, amongst other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the Constitution between the two rival Governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action of this court is indirect; it serves to resolve disputes about the exact limits of federal authority and prevent submission of these questions to state courts that might be partisan or partial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogatives of the Federal Government (enumerated executive and national functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was granted to the Union. The Union was also invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads which were to establish communication between different parts of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the independence of each State is recognized in its sphere, the Federal Government is authorized to interfere in internal affairs in a few predetermined cases where state independence might compromise the security of the Union at large.
